title: Chef Ranveer Brar's Crispy Chicken Popcorn Is the Monsoon Snack You Need Right Now
excerpt: The MasterChef India judge's cornflakes-coated chicken bites, paired with a garlicky cheese dip, offer a crunchy upgrade to the classic rainy-day snack.
body:
As monsoon rains sweep across India, few things satisfy quite like a plate of piping-hot fried chicken paired with a cup of masala chai. Chef Ranveer Brar, the Lucknow-born celebrity chef and MasterChef India judge, has shared his recipe for crispy chicken popcorn — a dish he positions as the perfect rainy-day indulgence.

Posted on his official channels, Brar's recipe transforms boneless chicken breast into golden, bite-sized morsels with a distinctly Indian spice profile and an unexpected coating ingredient: crushed cornflakes.

The Recipe: Indian Spices Meet Cornflakes Crunch

Brar's chicken popcorn begins with small cubes of boneless chicken breast marinated in a blend of degi red chilli powder, turmeric, coriander powder, a pinch of asafoetida, vinegar, chopped coriander leaves, and ginger-garlic paste. An egg white and cornstarch are folded in to bind the marinade and create a base layer of crispness.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=_gf89rtle4Q

The signature move comes in the coating. Rather than relying solely on breadcrumbs, Brar crushes cornflakes and mixes them with breadcrumbs to create a textured crust that fries up shatteringly crisp. Each marinated cube is rolled through this mixture before being slid into medium-hot oil and deep-fried in batches until evenly golden — roughly 15 to 20 minutes of cooking time.

"One by one coat the chicken cubes into the corn flakes crumb properly. Gently slide the pieces one after the other to the oil."

— Ranveer Brar, on his chicken popcorn technique

The finished popcorn is drained on absorbent paper and garnished with a coriander sprig and lemon wedge.

The Dip That Makes It

Where many chicken popcorn recipes default to ketchup, Brar pairs his with a homemade garlic-cheese-mayo dip. Raw garlic cloves, a broken green chilli, and fresh coriander leaves are blended with olive oil into a rough paste. This is stirred into mayonnaise along with grated cheese and black pepper, creating a rich, pungent counterpoint to the crispy chicken.

The entire recipe, from marination to plating, takes about 25 to 30 minutes and serves two — a manageable weeknight project that requires no specialty equipment beyond a kadai for deep-frying.

Why Monsoon Drives India's Fried-Snack Obsession

Brar's timing is deliberate. The Indian monsoon season, which typically runs from June through September, has long been associated with hot, fried snacks. Pakoras, bhajias, and samosas dominate street corners and home kitchens across the country as temperatures drop and humidity rises. The cultural connection between rain and fried food runs deep — it is as much about comfort and nostalgia as it is about appetite.

Chicken popcorn, a dish that originated in American fast-food chains, has found an enthusiastic audience in India. Street vendors and home cooks have adapted it with local spices — garam masala, Kashmiri chilli powder, chaat masala — turning it into something distinctly subcontinental. Brar's version, with its hing-spiked marinade and cornflakes armor, sits squarely in this tradition of Indian reinvention.

A Chef Who Bridges Street Food and Fine Dining

Ranveer Brar's culinary career spans more than two decades and multiple continents. Born in Lucknow, he apprenticed under kebab master Munir Ustad as a teenager before training at the Institute of Hotel Management. He became one of India's youngest executive chefs at 25, later opening the award-winning restaurants BanQ and Kashmir in Boston. BanQ was named one of the best new restaurants in the world by Wallpaper magazine.

After returning to India, Brar became a household name through television shows including The Great Indian Rasoi and his tenure as a judge on MasterChef India. His YouTube channel, where he shares recipes ranging from elaborate Lucknowi biryanis to quick everyday dishes, has become a go-to resource for home cooks in the Indian diaspora.

Worth Trying at Home

For diaspora cooks looking to recreate monsoon comfort food abroad, Brar's chicken popcorn is a practical starting point. All ingredients — cornflakes, breadcrumbs, standard Indian spices — are available at most grocery stores. The cornflakes coating is the detail worth paying attention to: it produces a noticeably crunchier result than breadcrumbs alone, and the pieces hold their texture longer, making the dish viable for gatherings where food sits out.

The full ingredient list calls for three chicken breasts, degi red chilli powder, turmeric, coriander powder, asafoetida, vinegar, ginger-garlic paste, egg white, cornstarch, cornflakes, and breadcrumbs. The dip requires garlic, green chilli, coriander, olive oil, cheese, mayonnaise, and black pepper.
